chapters.n: Paul writes to his trusted companion Timothy, now leading the Church in Ephesus. This is one of the three “Pastoral Epistles” (1 and 2 Timothy, Titus), letters of counsel to Church leaders.

f.g: Paul’s apostleship was assigned by God, not self-chosen.

chapters.n: Timothy is Paul’s “true son in the faith” — Paul likely taught and converted him. Paul adds “mercy” to his usual greeting of grace and peace.

f.w: my own son in the faith

chapters.n: As Paul left for Macedonia, he urged Timothy to stay in Ephesus and command certain people to stop teaching false doctrine.
They should stop obsessing over myths and endless family lineages, which lead to speculation rather than to God’s faith-based work of building people up.

f.g: Probably speculative lists of ancestors or spiritual beings used to build fanciful doctrines.

chapters.n: The goal of all this instruction is love flowing from a pure heart, a clear conscience, and sincere faith.
Some have drifted from these and wandered into meaningless talk.
They want to be experts in the law of Moses, but they don’t understand what they say or what they so confidently assert.
The law itself is good when it is used for its proper purpose.
The law wasn’t given mainly for the righteous but to restrain the lawless and rebellious — the godless, sinful, unholy, and those who would kill their own parents or anyone else.

It is for the sexually immoral, those who practice homosexual acts, kidnappers and slave-traders, liars, perjurers, and anything else contrary to healthy doctrine. The list roughly follows the Ten Commandments.
This standard agrees with the glorious gospel of the blessed God that was entrusted to Paul.
Paul thanks Christ for strengthening him, trusting him, and appointing him to serve.
Paul once insulted Christ, persecuted His followers, and acted violently. Yet he received mercy, because he acted in ignorance and unbelief.
The Lord’s grace overflowed to him, along with the faith and love found in Christ.
A trustworthy saying: Christ came into the world to save sinners — and Paul counts himself the worst of them. The greatest sinner can be saved.

f.g: A trustworthy saying — a phrase found only in the Pastoral Epistles.

chapters.n: That is why Christ showed Paul such patience: to make him an example for everyone who would later believe and gain eternal life.
Paul bursts into praise of the eternal King, immortal and unseen, the only wise God.

f.g: Unseen by mortal eyes except as He reveals Himself.

chapters.n: Paul entrusts this charge to Timothy, in line with earlier inspired prophecies about him, so that he can fight the good fight.

f.w: prophecies which went before on thee

chapters.n: Keep faith and a good conscience. Some have thrown away their conscience and wrecked their faith like a ship on the rocks.

f.g: A vivid image from Paul, who had been shipwrecked several times.

chapters.n: Hymenaeus and Alexander are examples. Paul has cut them off from the Church — handing them over to Satan’s domain outside the protection of the Saints — hoping they will learn to stop blaspheming.

f.g: Excommunicated, put outside the Church’s fellowship.

chapters.n: First of all, Paul urges prayers of every kind — requests, intercessions, and thanksgiving — for all people.
Pray for rulers and officials, so believers can live peaceful, quiet lives of godliness and dignity. Paul asks this even under pagan emperors.
This is good and pleasing to God our Savior.
God wants all people to be saved and to come to know the truth. Latter-day Saints see this desire fulfilled in missionary work and in work for the dead.
There is one God and only one Mediator between God and humanity — Jesus Christ, who became a man. He stands between us and the Father to reconcile us.
He gave Himself as a ransom for everyone — the price paid to free captives — and this was testified at the proper time.

f.g: At the right time in God’s plan.

chapters.n: Paul was appointed to proclaim this as a preacher, apostle, and teacher to the Gentiles. He insists he is telling the truth.
Paul wants the men everywhere to pray, lifting up hands that are clean, free from anger and arguing. Raising hands was a common posture of prayer.
Likewise women should dress modestly and sensibly, not trying to attract attention with elaborate hairstyles, gold, pearls, or expensive clothes — displays of wealth common among elite Roman women.
Instead, their true adornment should be good works, which fits women who profess to follow God.

Paul says a woman should learn quietly and with submission. Notably, he says women should learn — not always assumed in that culture. Many scholars read this as addressing specific disruptions in Ephesus.

f.g: Greek hēsychia — quietness, calm, not total speechlessness (the same word is in v. 2).

chapters.n: Paul does not permit a woman to teach or take authority over a man in the Ephesian assemblies. Interpreters differ on how broadly he meant this; elsewhere Paul honored women who prophesied, prayed, and labored in the gospel.

f.g: Greek authentein — a rare word, possibly meaning to domineer or seize authority.

chapters.n: Paul supports his point from the order of Creation: Adam was formed first, then Eve.
Eve was the one deceived by the serpent. Restoration scripture adds that Eve later rejoiced in the Fall as the way to bring children and redemption, giving a more hopeful view of her role.
Yet women will be saved through childbearing — or, many think, through “the Childbirth,” Christ’s birth — if they continue in faith, love, holiness, and self-control.

f.g: Greek has “the childbearing”; possibly a reference to the birth of Christ, the promised seed.

chapters.n: A trustworthy saying: wanting to serve as a bishop is wanting a good work. In the early Church, the bishop was an overseer who presided over a local congregation.

f.g: Greek episkopos — overseer; one who watches over the flock.

chapters.n: A bishop must have an unblemished reputation, be faithful to his wife, self-controlled, sensible, respectable, welcoming, and able to teach.

f.g: A faithful, one-woman man; likely ruling out unfaithfulness or polygamy in that setting.

chapters.n: He must not be a heavy drinker or violent, but gentle and peaceable, not greedy or quarrelsome, and not in love with money.

f.g: Not violent, not quick to hit.

chapters.n: He must lead his own family well, with children who respect him.
If a man can’t lead his own household, how can he care for God’s Church? The family is the training ground for leadership.
He must not be a new convert, or he could become conceited and fall under the same judgment as the devil, whose downfall was pride.
He must also have a good reputation with outsiders, so he isn’t disgraced and trapped by the devil.
Deacons, too, must be serious and worthy of respect, honest in speech, not heavy drinkers, and not greedy.

f.g: Greek diakonoi — servants, assistants to the bishop.
Saying one thing to one person and another to someone else.

chapters.n: They must hold fast to the revealed truths of the faith with a clear conscience.

f.g: The revealed truths of the gospel.

chapters.n: They should first be tested, and if found blameless, then serve as deacons.
Likewise the women — likely deacons’ wives, or possibly women who served the Church — must be dignified, not gossips, self-controlled, and faithful in everything.

f.g: Greek gynaikas — “women” or “wives”; context is debated.
Greek diabolous — the word also used for “devil.”

chapters.n: Deacons must be faithful husbands who lead their children and households well.
Those who serve well as deacons earn a good standing and great confidence in their faith in Christ.

f.g: A good standing, an honorable position.

chapters.n: Paul hopes to come to Timothy soon, but writes these instructions now.
If Paul is delayed, Timothy will know how people should conduct themselves in God’s household — the Church of the living God, which supports and upholds the truth.

f.g: God’s household or family, not a building.

f.w: pillar and ground of the truth
f.g: Support and foundation that hold truth up.

chapters.n: Paul quotes what may be an early hymn about Christ: God came in the flesh, was vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, preached to the nations, believed in by the world, and taken up into glory.

f.w: God was manifest in the flesh

f.g: Vindicated — shown to be right — by the Spirit, especially in the Resurrection.

chapters.n: The Spirit plainly warns that in later times some will abandon the faith, following deceptive spirits and teachings that come from devils. This is another prophecy of apostasy.
These teachings come through hypocritical liars whose consciences are numb, as if cauterized with a branding iron.

f.g: Cauterized — burned until it can no longer feel.

chapters.n: They forbid marriage and demand abstaining from certain foods — things God created to be enjoyed with gratitude by believers. Latter-day revelation also rejects forbidding marriage.
Everything God created is good, and nothing should be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving.

f.w: every creature of God is good

chapters.n: It is made holy by God’s word and by prayer — as when we bless our food.
If Timothy reminds the members of these things, he will be a good servant of Christ, nourished by the faith and sound doctrine he has followed.
Don’t waste time on irreverent myths and silly old wives’ tales; train yourself instead in godliness, like an athlete.

f.g: Greek gymnaze — train, as in a gymnasium.

chapters.n: Physical training has some value, but spiritual training benefits everything, promising blessings in this life and the next.

f.w: the life that now is, and of that which is to come

chapters.n: Another trustworthy saying that deserves full acceptance.
This is why we work hard and endure criticism: our hope is in the living God, the Savior of all people — especially of those who believe.
Paul tells Timothy to command and teach these things with confidence.
Timothy was probably in his thirties — young for a leader. Paul says not to let anyone look down on his youth, but to be a model for believers in speech, conduct, love, faith, and purity.
Until Paul arrives, Timothy should focus on the public reading of scripture, on preaching, and on teaching doctrine — the main parts of early Church meetings.

f.g: Public reading of scripture in Church meetings.

chapters.n: Don’t neglect your spiritual gift, which came through prophecy when the elders laid their hands on you. This describes ordination by the laying on of hands.
Think deeply about these things and give yourself fully to them, so your progress is visible to everyone.
Watch your own life and your teaching closely, and persist. Doing this will save both you and those you teach.

f.w: save thyself, and them that hear thee

chapters.n: Treat Church members like family. Don’t harshly scold an older man; appeal to him respectfully as you would your father, and treat younger men as brothers.

f.g: Sharply reprimand, strike at with words.

chapters.n: Treat older women as mothers and younger women as sisters, with complete purity.

f.g: Keeping relationships chaste and above suspicion.

chapters.n: Honor and support widows who are truly alone and in need. In that world widows often had no income and depended on family or charity.

f.g: Truly destitute widows with no family to help.

chapters.n: If a widow has children or grandchildren, they should first learn to show devotion at home by caring for her and repaying their parents. That pleases God.
A true widow who is left alone puts her hope in God and keeps praying night and day.
But a widow who lives for pleasure is spiritually dead even while she lives.
Give these instructions to the Saints so no one can criticize them.
Anyone who doesn’t care for their relatives, especially their own household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever — since even pagans cared for family.
To be enrolled on the Church’s list of supported widows, a woman should be at least sixty and have been faithful to her husband.
She should be known for good works: raising children, showing hospitality, humbly serving the Saints, helping the suffering, and devoting herself to doing good.
Don’t enroll younger widows. When their natural desires draw them away from their dedication to Christ, they will want to remarry.
They would then bring judgment on themselves for breaking their earlier pledge — likely a promise of service made when enrolled.
Supported but unoccupied, they may also become idle, going from house to house gossiping and meddling.
So Paul counsels younger widows to remarry, raise children, manage their homes, and give enemies no reason to criticize the Church.
Some have already turned away to follow Satan.
Any believer with widows in the family should support them so the Church isn’t burdened and can help the widows who truly have no one.
Elders who lead well deserve double honor — respect and fair support — especially those who work hard at preaching and teaching.

f.g: Generous respect and, likely, material support.

chapters.n: Paul quotes Moses — don’t muzzle an ox while it works the grain — and a saying of Jesus that a worker deserves his pay.

f.w: Thou shalt not muzzle the ox
The labourer is worthy of his reward

chapters.n: Don’t accept an accusation against an elder unless two or three witnesses support it — protecting leaders from rumor.
Those who continue in sin should be corrected publicly, so others will be warned.

f.g: Correct openly, in front of the congregation.

chapters.n: Paul solemnly charges Timothy, before God, Christ, and the chosen angels, to apply these rules impartially, without favoritism.
Don’t be hasty in ordaining anyone by the laying on of hands, or you will share responsibility for their sins. Keep yourself pure.
A personal aside: stop drinking only water; use a little wine for your stomach and frequent illnesses. Water was often unsafe, and wine was a common remedy.

f.g: Medicinal advice in a world before modern sanitation; the Word of Wisdom came much later.

chapters.n: Some people’s sins are obvious and announce their judgment ahead of time; others’ sins only come out later. This helps explain v. 22: take time before ordaining.
Likewise, some good deeds are obvious, and even those that aren’t cannot stay hidden forever. Time reveals character.
Slaves who are believers should respect their masters, so that God’s name and the gospel won’t be slandered. Paul is concerned with the Church’s witness in a society built on slavery.
Those with believing masters shouldn’t disrespect them for being fellow members; they should serve even better, since the masters benefiting are beloved believers.

f.g: Those who receive the benefit of the service.

chapters.n: If anyone teaches something different and rejects the healthy words of Jesus Christ and godly doctrine —
— he is puffed up and understands nothing. He has an unhealthy craving for controversy and word-fights, which produce envy, quarrels, insults, and evil suspicions.
and constant friction among people with corrupted minds who have lost the truth and think religion is a way to make money. Stay away from them.

f.g: Thinking religion is a means of profit.

chapters.n: True gain is godliness combined with contentment.

f.g: Being satisfied with what you have.

chapters.n: We brought nothing into this world, and we can take nothing out of it.

f.w: we brought nothing into this world

chapters.n: If we have food and clothing, we will be content with that.
But those determined to be rich fall into temptation and traps, and into foolish, harmful desires that sink people into ruin.

f.g: Those who set their hearts on getting rich.

chapters.n: The love of money is a root of every kind of evil. Some, longing for it, have wandered from the faith and stabbed themselves with many griefs. Note: money itself isn’t condemned, but loving it.
But you, man of God, run from these things. Pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, endurance, and gentleness.

f.g: A title used for prophets in the Old Testament.

chapters.n: Fight the good fight of faith; seize eternal life, to which you were called when you made your confession of faith before many witnesses — perhaps at his baptism or ordination.

f.g: Contend in the noble contest, as an athlete.

chapters.n: Paul solemnly charges Timothy before God, who gives life to everything, and before Christ, who bore faithful witness before Pontius Pilate.
Keep this commandment spotless and beyond reproach until Jesus Christ appears.
God will bring about Christ’s appearing at His own appointed time. He is the blessed and only Sovereign, King of kings and Lord of lords.

f.w: King of kings, and Lord of lords

chapters.n: He alone has immortality and dwells in unapproachable light. The JST clarifies that no man can approach Him except “he who hath the light and the hope of immortality dwelling in him” — echoing that the righteous can see God.

f.w: whom no man hath seen, nor can see

chapters.n: Tell those who are rich in this world not to be arrogant or trust in uncertain wealth, but in the living God, who richly gives us everything to enjoy.
They should do good, be rich in good deeds, generous, and willing to share.
That way they store up treasure as a solid foundation for the future and lay hold of real, eternal life.
Timothy, guard what has been entrusted to you. Avoid irreverent empty talk and the contradictions of what is falsely called “knowledge.”

f.w: that which is committed to thy trust
f.g: The deposit — the gospel entrusted to him.
Greek gnōsis — knowledge; here, false spiritual “knowledge,” not modern science.

chapters.n: Some who claimed such knowledge have wandered from the faith. Paul ends with grace.
